title: Chanticleer and Partlet: How Partlet Died and Was Buried, and How Chanticleer Died of Grief
paragraphs: On another day Chanticleer and Partlet agreed to go up into the mountains again to eat nuts, and they settled that any nuts they found would be shared equally. Partlet found a very large nut, but she said nothing to Chanticleer about it and kept it all for herself. It was so big, though, that she could not swallow it, and it stuck in her throat. She was terrified and cried out to Chanticleer, “Please run as fast as you can and fetch me some water, or I will choke!” Chanticleer ran as fast as he could to the river and said, “River, give me some water, because Partlet is lying on the mountain and will choke on a big nut.” The river answered, “First run to the bride and ask her for a silken cord to draw the water up.” Chanticleer ran to the bride and said, “Bride, you must give me a silken cord, because then the river will give me water, and I will carry the water to Partlet, who is lying on the mountain and will choke on a big nut.” But the bride said, “First run and bring me my garland, which is hanging on a willow in the garden.” So Chanticleer ran to the garden, took the garland from the branch where it hung, and brought it to the bride. Then the bride gave him the silken cord, and he took the silken cord to the river, and the river gave him water, and he carried the water to Partlet. But in the meantime she had choked on the big nut, and she lay quite dead and never moved again.

Chanticleer was heartbroken and cried bitterly, and all the animals came and wept with him over poor Partlet. Six mice built a little hearse to carry her to her grave, and when it was finished they harnessed themselves to the front of it, and Chanticleer drove them. On the way they met the fox. “Where are you going, Chanticleer?” he asked. “To bury my Partlet,” said Chanticleer. “May I come with you?” asked the fox. “Yes, but you must climb up on the back, or my horses won’t be able to pull you.” So the fox climbed up on the back, and soon the wolf, the bear, the goat and all the other animals of the wood came and climbed onto the hearse as well.

So they went on until they came to a fast stream. “How will we get across?” said Chanticleer. A straw said, “I will lay myself across, and you can cross over on me.” But as the mice were crossing, the straw slid away and fell into the water, and all six mice fell in and drowned. What was to be done? Then a big log came and said, “I am large enough. I will lay myself across the stream, and you can cross over on me.” So he lay down across it, but they went about it so clumsily that the log fell in and was swept away by the current. Then a stone, who had seen what happened, came over and kindly offered to help poor Chanticleer by lying across the stream. This time Chanticleer got safely to the other side with the hearse and managed to pull Partlet out of it. But the fox and the other mourners, who were sitting at the back, were too heavy. They fell back into the water and were all swept away and drowned.

So Chanticleer was left alone with his dead Partlet. He dug a grave for her, laid her in it, and heaped a little mound over her. Then he sat down beside the grave and wept and mourned until at last he died too. And so everyone was dead.
